blocks.content: 1. Three Words That Sound Similar, Measure Completely Different Things
blocks.text: 1. Three Words That Sound Similar, Measure Completely Different Things

blocks.content: Latency, throughput, and bandwidth get confused constantly, and confusing them leads directly to wrong diagnoses and wrong fixes: throwing more bandwidth at a latency problem, or trying to speed up individual requests when the real issue is capacity.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271963437-387958934.png
blocks.alt: Three genuinely different questions, each with its own unit and its own fix

blocks.content: {"headers":["Concept","Question It Answers","Typical Unit"],"rows":[["Latency","How long does one request take, start to finish?","Milliseconds (ms)"],["Throughput","How many requests can the system handle per second?","Requests per second (req/s)"],["Bandwidth","How much data could flow through the connection at once?","Bits per second (Mbps, Gbps)"]]}
2. Latency: How Long Does One Thing Take?
blocks.text: 2. Latency: How Long Does One Thing Take?

blocks.content: Latency is the time it takes for a single request to travel from the sender to the destination and get a response back, a measure of speed from one user's perspective. If you click Search and results appear after 200ms, that 200ms is your latency.
Latency Has Layers Inside It
blocks.text: Latency Has Layers Inside It

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025890-995044326.png
blocks.alt: The total latency a user feels is the sum of several smaller delays stacked one after another

blocks.content: The total latency a user feels is the sum of many smaller delays: network travel time to reach the server, queueing and processing time once it arrives, time spent waiting on a database or downstream service call, and the return trip back to the user. A slowdown in any single layer adds directly to what the user experiences.
How Latency Is Measured in Practice
blocks.text: How Latency Is Measured in Practice

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271967385-328723811.png
blocks.alt: A single average number can look perfectly healthy while hiding a genuinely painful experience for a meaningful slice of users

blocks.content: A single average number hides a lot, which is why engineers look at percentiles instead: p50 (the median), p95, and p99 (the tail).

blocks.title: Never Trust Average Latency Alone
blocks.content: If 99% of requests finish in 10ms but 1% take 10 seconds, the average still looks fine while real users in that 1% are genuinely suffering. Always look at p95 and p99 in production, not just the average.
3. Throughput: How Much Can the System Handle?
blocks.text: 3. Throughput: How Much Can the System Handle?

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271969122-826835574.png
blocks.alt: Throughput measures capacity, and stays the same number regardless of how fast or slow any individual request happens to be

blocks.content: Throughput is the number of requests, operations, or units of work a system can process per unit of time, a measure of capacity, not speed. A system processing 5,000 API calls per second has a throughput of 5,000 req/s, whether each individual call takes 10ms or 100ms doesn't change that throughput number, it changes latency instead.
Throughput vs Capacity
blocks.text: Throughput vs Capacity

blocks.content: Throughput is what a system actually achieves under real load. Capacity is the theoretical maximum. The two are rarely equal, real systems have queueing, garbage collection pauses, network jitter, and lock contention that a purely theoretical capacity number never accounts for.
Little's Law
blocks.text: Little's Law

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271970953-384550798.png
blocks.alt: Little's Law ties concurrency, latency, and throughput into a single, exact relationship

blocks.content: Little's Law: Throughput = Concurrency / Latency. If a system handles 100 concurrent requests and each takes 20ms, throughput = 100 / 0.02 = 5,000 req/s. This relationship means latency and throughput are directly connected, you cannot change one without affecting the others, a fact section 6 explores through some of its most common misconceptions.
4. Bandwidth: How Wide Is the Pipe?
blocks.text: 4. Bandwidth: How Wide Is the Pipe?

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271972683-9354556.png
blocks.alt: Bandwidth is the ceiling on how much data could flow, not a measurement of how much is actually flowing right now

blocks.content: Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data that can flow through a network link per second, the theoretical ceiling, how wide the pipe is, not how fast water moves through it or how much water is actually being sent at any given moment.

A 1 Gbps network link can carry up to one gigabit of data per second. Whether you are actually using 10 Mbps or 900 Mbps of that link right now is utilization, a separate, dynamic measurement, not the bandwidth figure itself, which stays fixed regardless of current usage.
5. Seeing All Three at Once: The Highway Analogy
blocks.text: 5. Seeing All Three at Once: The Highway Analogy

blocks.content: The single best way to feel all three concepts together: imagine a highway representing a network connection.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271974593-42003085.png
blocks.alt: A highway maps each of the three concepts onto something physically intuitive

blocks.content: ["Bandwidth is the highway's width, how many lanes exist. A wider highway lets more cars travel side by side at the same time, without changing how fast any individual car moves","Latency is one car's own travel time from the start of the highway to the end. A car doing 120 km/h with a clear road has low latency; traffic lights, speed limits, or congestion raise it","Throughput is how many cars pass a fixed checkpoint every minute, and it depends on both of the other two: faster cars (lower latency) pass the checkpoint more often, and more lanes (higher bandwidth) let more cars pass side by side at once"]
items: Bandwidth is the highway's width, how many lanes exist. A wider highway lets more cars travel side by side at the same time, without changing how fast any individual car moves
Latency is one car's own travel time from the start of the highway to the end. A car doing 120 km/h with a clear road has low latency; traffic lights, speed limits, or congestion raise it

Throughput is how many cars pass a fixed checkpoint every minute, and it depends on both of the other two: faster cars (lower latency) pass the checkpoint more often, and more lanes (higher bandwidth) let more cars pass side by side at once

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271976367-341757938.png
blocks.alt: The same highway can combine bandwidth and latency in very different ways, and only one combination actually produces high throughput

blocks.content: A ten-lane highway with barely-moving traffic (high bandwidth, high latency due to construction) still produces disappointingly low throughput. A narrow, single-lane highway with cars moving extremely fast (low bandwidth, low latency) is throughput-limited for a completely different reason, simply not enough room for many cars at once. Only a wide highway with genuinely fast-moving traffic produces high throughput, this is exactly why bandwidth and throughput are not the same thing, and why fixing only one of the two rarely fixes a throughput problem on its own.
6. How They Relate, and Where People Get Confused
blocks.text: 6. How They Relate, and Where People Get Confused

blocks.content: The three are connected but independent. Changing one does not automatically fix the others, and these four confusions account for most of the wrong diagnoses made in practice.
1. More Bandwidth Does Not Mean Lower Latency
blocks.text: 1. More Bandwidth Does Not Mean Lower Latency

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271978055-593235110.png
blocks.alt: A wider pipe moves more data at once, it does not make any single piece of data travel faster

blocks.content: Misconception: increasing bandwidth makes requests faster. Reality: bandwidth only increases how much data can be transferred at once, it does not reduce the travel time of individual packets. A 10 Gbps connection between New York and London still has roughly 70ms of latency, because that number is bounded by the physical speed of light over that distance, not by how wide the pipe is.
2. Low Latency Does Not Mean High Throughput
blocks.text: 2. Low Latency Does Not Mean High Throughput

blocks.content: Misconception: if requests are fast, the system can handle many of them. Reality: a system can respond very quickly while only processing one request at a time. A single-threaded server might respond in 5ms but still handle only a small number of requests per second overall, because throughput depends on concurrency and parallelism, not just how fast any one response is.
3. High Throughput Does Not Mean a Fast System
blocks.text: 3. High Throughput Does Not Mean a Fast System

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271979702-652765799.png
blocks.alt: A system can process an enormous volume of work per second while every individual user still waits a long time for their own request

blocks.content: Misconception: a system handling many requests per second is always fast. Reality: it may process a large total volume, while individual users still experience long wait times. A queue processing 10,000 requests per second is a genuinely large throughput number, but if each individual request waits 30 seconds in that queue before being handled, high throughput has clearly not guaranteed low latency.
4. Bandwidth Is Not Always the Bottleneck
blocks.text: 4. Bandwidth Is Not Always the Bottleneck

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025892-302334223.png
blocks.alt: Most everyday web applications hit a CPU or database limit long before they ever come close to exhausting their network bandwidth

blocks.content: Misconception: most performance problems come from limited network bandwidth. Reality: many systems hit CPU, memory, database, or disk limits long before they ever exhaust their network capacity. An e-commerce site can become slow purely because its database is overloaded, while the network itself sits barely used. For most web applications, CPU and database performance are the bigger bottleneck, bandwidth becomes genuinely critical mainly for video streaming, large file transfers, and large-scale data or ML workloads.
7. What Causes High Latency?
blocks.text: 7. What Causes High Latency?

blocks.content: High latency is almost always traceable to one of five common root causes, and knowing which one you are actually dealing with is what tells you the right fix.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271983045-422298638.png
blocks.alt: Five recurring root causes behind most real-world latency problems

blocks.content: {"headers":["Root Cause","What It Looks Like"],"rows":[["Network distance and hops","Requests crossing regions or continents, or passing through unnecessary intermediate services"],["Server-side queueing under load","Requests waiting for a free thread or worker once concurrent load exceeds what the server can process immediately"],["Slow downstream dependencies","A single request fanning out to several other services, each adding its own delay to the total"],["Unindexed or expensive database queries","A query that should take milliseconds instead scanning far more rows than necessary"],["Serialization and payload size","Large JSON payloads or inefficient serialization formats adding real processing time before a byte is even sent"]]}
8. How to Improve Each One
blocks.text: 8. How to Improve Each One

blocks.content: Latency is improved by making individual requests faster, throughput by processing more requests in parallel, and bandwidth by increasing the amount of data that can be transferred per unit of time, three genuinely different engineering problems with three genuinely different sets of fixes.
Reduce Latency (Make Each Request Faster)
blocks.text: Reduce Latency (Make Each Request Faster)

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271984612-935594315.png
blocks.alt: Latency fixes generally shorten the path a request has to travel or the work it has to wait on

blocks.content: ["Caching (Redis, a CDN): serve frequently accessed data from memory instead of fetching it repeatedly from the database","Move compute closer to users: edge servers or a CDN so requests travel a shorter physical distance","Reduce the number of downstream hops a single request depends on, each additional hop adds its own delay on top of every other"]
items: Caching (Redis, a CDN): serve frequently accessed data from memory instead of fetching it repeatedly from the database
Move compute closer to users: edge servers or a CDN so requests travel a shorter physical distance
Reduce the number of downstream hops a single request depends on, each additional hop adds its own delay on top of every other

blocks.content: Increase Throughput (Handle More Requests)
blocks.text: Increase Throughput (Handle More Requests)

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271986245-50887413.png
blocks.alt: Throughput fixes generally add more parallel capacity rather than making any single request faster

blocks.content: ["Horizontal scaling: add more servers to share the workload","Increase concurrency: more threads, async I/O, or event-driven architectures to process multiple requests simultaneously","Queue and batch work where the use case allows it, trading a small amount of latency for significantly higher sustained throughput"]

Increase concurrency: more threads, async I/O, or event-driven architectures to process multiple requests simultaneously
Queue and batch work where the use case allows it, trading a small amount of latency for significantly higher sustained throughput

blocks.content: Increase Bandwidth (Transfer More Data)
blocks.text: Increase Bandwidth (Transfer More Data)

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271987814-125122399.png
blocks.alt: Bandwidth fixes generally widen the pipe itself or reduce how much needs to travel through it

Compress data before transmission, effectively increasing how much useful data fits through the existing bandwidth
Use a CDN to shorten the physical path data has to travel, reducing how much of the available bandwidth is spent purely on distance

blocks.content: 9. Bandwidth-Delay Product: Where Bandwidth and Latency Interact
blocks.text: 9. Bandwidth-Delay Product: Where Bandwidth and Latency Interact

blocks.content: Bandwidth and latency are independent, but one specific quantity, the bandwidth-delay product, or BDP, depends on both at once, and explains a real, common performance problem on high-latency links.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271989374-691590620.png
blocks.alt: BDP tells you exactly how much data needs to be in flight to keep a high-bandwidth, high-latency link fully utilized

blocks.content: BDP = Bandwidth x Round-Trip Time, the amount of data that can be in flight, sent but not yet acknowledged, at any given moment for the link to stay fully utilized. A 1 Gbps link with a 100ms round trip has a BDP of roughly 12.5 MB, meaning a sender needs that much data outstanding at once to actually use the full gigabit of available bandwidth.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271990932-165450541.png
blocks.alt: A TCP send window sized for a low-latency link becomes a bottleneck the moment that same bandwidth is paired with high latency instead

blocks.content: This is exactly why a connection with plenty of bandwidth can still transfer data slowly over a high-latency path: if TCP's send window is smaller than the link's BDP, the sender runs out of data it is allowed to have outstanding and has to pause, waiting for acknowledgments before sending more, leaving the link's own bandwidth sitting unused in the gaps. This is precisely the reason satellite links and long-distance transcontinental transfers need explicitly tuned, larger TCP window sizes to actually achieve their theoretical bandwidth, a genuinely different fix from either a pure latency problem or a pure bandwidth upgrade.
10. Which One to Optimize For?
blocks.text: 10. Which One to Optimize For?

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271992660-820069705.png
blocks.alt: The right answer depends entirely on what the system does and who, or what, is waiting on the result

blocks.content: The answer depends entirely on what your system does and who is waiting. Real-time trading systems, multiplayer games, and voice or video calls need latency optimized first, users feel every extra millisecond directly. Bulk data processing and analytics pipelines need throughput optimized first, nobody is watching a single record process in real time, but the total volume processed per hour matters enormously. Video streaming and large file transfer systems need bandwidth optimized first, since the sheer volume of data moved is the actual constraint.

Most production systems need a working balance of all three, not a maximum of just one, an API that is blazingly low-latency but falls over the moment traffic doubles has simply traded one failure mode for another.

The example below implements Little's Law directly, exactly as introduced in section 3, and uses it to reproduce two of this topic's own numbers: the 100-concurrent-requests-at-20ms example that yields 5,000 req/s, and the misconception #3 queueing example, where a system sustaining 10,000 req/s of throughput but making each request wait 30 seconds implies a genuinely enormous number of requests in flight at once, concretely showing why high throughput alone says nothing about whether any individual user is having a good experience.

codes.python:
# Little's Law: throughput = concurrency / latency (latency in seconds).
def throughput(concurrency, latency_seconds):
    return concurrency / latency_seconds


# Rearranged: concurrency = throughput * latency.
def concurrency_in_flight(throughput_per_second, latency_seconds):
    return throughput_per_second * latency_seconds


def main():
    example1_throughput = throughput(100, 0.020)
    print(f"100 concurrent requests at 20ms each: {example1_throughput:.0f} req/s")

    queue_latency_seconds = 30.0
    sustained_throughput = 10000
    in_flight = concurrency_in_flight(sustained_throughput, queue_latency_seconds)
    print(f"10,000 req/s sustained with 30s latency implies {in_flight:.0f} requests in flight at once")

    # Doubling throughput while holding latency fixed doubles required concurrency too.
    doubled_throughput = sustained_throughput * 2
    in_flight_at_doubled = concurrency_in_flight(doubled_throughput, queue_latency_seconds)
    print(f"Doubling that throughput to {doubled_throughput:.0f} req/s at the same latency needs {in_flight_at_doubled:.0f} requests in flight")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: Worked Example 1: Video Calls vs Payroll Processing
blocks.text: Worked Example 1: Video Calls vs Payroll Processing

blocks.content: A video call platform and a batch payroll processing system both claim to be well-engineered, but they optimize for entirely different things. The video call platform lives or dies on latency, a 300ms round trip makes conversation feel broken, so it invests in edge servers, UDP-based transport, and the shortest possible network path, while treating its own throughput ceiling per server as a secondary concern since call volume per server is naturally limited by bandwidth per call anyway.

The payroll system processes millions of employee records once a month with no one watching any individual record's processing time in real time, so it optimizes overwhelmingly for throughput, batching records, running many workers in parallel, and accepting that any single record might sit in a queue for several minutes before being processed. Applying either system's optimization strategy to the other would be actively counterproductive, low-latency single-record processing would make the payroll run take dramatically longer overall, and batching video call frames for throughput would make every conversation unusable.
Worked Example 2: A Slow File Transfer Over a Satellite Link
blocks.text: Worked Example 2: A Slow File Transfer Over a Satellite Link

blocks.content: A company transfers backup files over a satellite link advertised at 50 Mbps, but real transfer speeds consistently measure closer to 5 Mbps. The link's round-trip time is unusually high, around 600ms, given the distance to a satellite in geostationary orbit, and its bandwidth-delay product from section 9 works out to roughly 3.75 MB, far larger than the sender's default TCP window size.

The team initially suspects the satellite link itself is underdelivering on bandwidth, but the real cause is exactly the BDP mismatch: the sender keeps pausing to wait for acknowledgments before its small window allows more data out, leaving most of the link's actual 50 Mbps capacity sitting idle between bursts. Increasing the TCP window size to match the link's BDP, rather than requesting more bandwidth from the satellite provider, is what actually fixes the transfer speed.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.content: A checkout API reports 8,000 req/s throughput and a team declares it fast. Using the concepts from sections 3 and 6, explain what additional single measurement you would demand before agreeing with that claim, and why.

Using Little's Law from section 3, if a system needs to sustain 2,000 req/s while keeping p99 latency under 100ms, calculate the minimum number of concurrent in-flight requests the system must be able to support, and explain what specifically happens if it is only provisioned to handle half that concurrency.

Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Key Takeaways

blocks.content: Latency, throughput, and bandwidth measure three genuinely different things: how long one request takes, how many requests a system handles per second, and how much data a connection could carry at once. They are related, Little's Law ties concurrency, latency, and throughput into one exact equation, but improving one does not automatically improve the others, and the four common misconceptions in section 6 are exactly where most wrong diagnoses come from in practice.

Which one to optimize for depends entirely on what the system does, real-time systems chase latency, bulk processing chases throughput, and data-heavy transfer chases bandwidth, with most production systems needing a working balance of all three rather than a maximum of just one. Together with the CAP Theorem, Consistency Models, and Reliability topics, these metrics complete the vocabulary this module uses to reason precisely about tradeoffs, rather than describing systems only in vague, qualitative terms.
